content: 1. Newly born infants who do not breathe spontaneously after thorough drying should be stimulated by gently rubbing their back 2–3 times before clamping the umbilical cord and initiating positive pressure ventilation. This is a weak recommendation, and the quality of evidence is not graded. 2. Routine nasal or oral suctioning should not be performed for infants born through clear amniotic fluid who begin breathing on their own after birth. This is a strong recommendation supported by high-quality evidence. 3. Intrapartum suctioning of the mouth and nose during the delivery of the head in neonates born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid is not recommended. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 4. Suctioning of the mouth or nose is not recommended in neonates born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid who begin breathing on their own. This is a weak recommendation, and the quality of evidence is not graded. 5. Tracheal suctioning should not be performed in newly born infants born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid who begin breathing on their own. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate to low-quality evidence. 6. In neonates born through clear amniotic fluid who do not start breathing after thorough drying and back rubbing 2–3 times, suctioning of the mouth and nose should not be routinely performed before initiating positive-pressure ventilation. Suctioning should only be done if the mouth or nose is full of secretions. This is a weak recommendation based on consensus in the absence of published evidence. 7. In neonates born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid who do not start breathing on their own, tracheal suctioning should be performed before initiating positive-pressure ventilation, but only in situations where endotracheal intubation is possible. This is a weak recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 8. In neonates born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid who do not start breathing on their own, suctioning of the mouth and nose should be performed before initiating positive-pressure ventilation. This is a weak recommendation based on consensus in the absence of published evidence. 9. Delayed cord clamping, performed 1–3 minutes after birth, is recommended for all births while simultaneously initiating essential newborn care. This is a strong recommendation supported by moderate-quality evidence. 10. Early cord clamping, defined as clamping within the first minute after birth, is not recommended unless the neonate is asphyxiated and requires immediate resuscitation. This is a strong recommendation supported by moderate-quality evidence. 11. Newborns without complications should be kept in skin-to-skin contact with their mothers during the first hour after birth to prevent hypothermia and promote breastfeeding. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 12. All newborns, including low-birth-weight infants who are able to breastfeed, should be put to the breast as soon as possible after birth when they are clinically stable, and both the mother and baby are ready. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 13. All newborns should receive 1 mg of vitamin K intramuscularly after birth, preferably after the first hour during which skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding initiation occur. This is a strong recommendation supported by moderate-quality evidence. 14. Neonates requiring surgical procedures, those with birth trauma, preterm newborns, and those exposed in utero to maternal medications that interfere with vitamin K are at particularly high risk of bleeding and must receive 1 mg of vitamin K intramuscularly. This is a strong recommendation supported by moderate-quality evidence. 15. After an uncomplicated vaginal birth in a health facility, healthy mothers and newborns should remain in the facility for at least 24 hours after birth to receive care. This is a weak recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 16. If birth occurs in a facility, the mother and newborn should receive postnatal care during the first 24 hours before discharge. If birth occurs at home, the first postnatal contact should occur as early as possible within 24 hours of birth. At least three additional postnatal contacts are recommended for all mothers and newborns: on day 3 (48–72 hours), between days 7–14, and at 6 weeks after birth. This is a strong recommendation supported by moderate-quality evidence for newborn outcomes and low-quality evidence for maternal outcomes. 17. Home visits during the first week after birth are recommended for the care of the mother and newborn. This is a strong recommendation supported by moderate-quality evidence for newborn outcomes and low-quality evidence for maternal outcomes. 18. All infants should be exclusively breastfed from birth until 6 months of age. Mothers should be counseled and supported for exclusive breastfeeding at each postnatal contact. This is a strong recommendation supported by moderate-quality evidence for neonatal outcomes, with the 6-month duration based on previous WHO recommendations and an updated Cochrane review. 19. Daily application of 4% chlorhexidine to the umbilical cord stump during the first week of life is recommended for newborns born at home in settings with high neonatal mortality (neonatal mortality rate >30 per 1,000). Clean, dry cord care is recommended for newborns born in health facilities and at home in low neonatal mortality settings. Chlorhexidine use in these situations may be considered only to replace harmful traditional substances, such as cow dung, applied to the cord stump. This is a strong situational recommendation supported by moderate-quality evidence. 20. Bathing should be delayed until at least 24 hours after birth. If this is not possible due to cultural reasons, bathing should be delayed for at least 6 hours. Appropriate clothing for the baby, consisting of 1–2 layers more than adults and a hat, is recommended. The mother and baby should not be separated and should remain in the same room 24 hours a day. This is a strong situational recommendation based on consensus. 21. All infants should receive their first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth, preferably within 24 hours. This is crucial in areas of high hepatitis B endemicity but remains important even in intermediate and low endemicity areas. This is a strong recommendation supported by moderate-quality evidence. 22. Oral polio vaccine, including a birth dose (referred to as zero dose because it does not count toward the primary series), is recommended in all polio-endemic countries and in countries at high risk for importation and subsequent spread. The birth dose should be administered at birth or as soon as possible thereafter. This is a strong recommendation supported by high-quality evidence.
